thread.title: Apple Will Buy Tesla --- and Other Wild Predictions for 2019

title: Apple Will Buy Tesla --- and Other Wild Predictions for 2019
text:
Apple Will Buy Tesla and Other Wild Predictions for 2019 By Updated Dec. 5, 2018 9:30 a.m. ET Order Reprints Photograph by Jack Taylor/Getty Images Text size
It’s that time of year—Christmas is just weeks away and the New Year beckons. Investment banks’ research departments and brokerage firms are busy putting out their 2019 investment outlooks. These documents—which sometimes reach into the hundreds of pages—are meant to guide clients through what the experts predict will be the market-moving forces in the year to come.
Danish trading and investment bank Saxo Bank has a different approach: In addition to a formal outlook and forecast, the Copenhagen-based firm puts out a series of “Outrageous Predictions.” These events are admittedly unlikely to occur but would have major investment implications if they did. Yet their point is to provoke debate, not to serve as explicit predictions.
For 2019’s list of 10 outrageous predictions , the bank settled on the theme of “Enough Is Enough,” as “a world running on empty will have to wake up and start creating reforms, not because it wants to but because it has to,” according to Saxo Bank Chief Economist Steen Jakobsen.
Years of individuals and institutions around the world piling on debt and populist political movements that continue to grow have culminated in a global focus on short-term gains at the expense of long-term growth. “We think 2019 will mark a profound pivot away from this mentality as we are reaching the end of the road in piling on new debt and next year will see us all beginning to pay the piper for our errant ways,” wrote Jakobsen in Saxo’s presentation.
But enough of that. Here are a few of Saxo’s more-outrageous predictions:
Apple “secures funding” for Tesla at $520 a share.
“What will Apple do next with its $237 billion cash-and-equivalents hoard and its important iPhone product line that is incapable of further volume growth?” asks Peter Garnry, Saxo’s head of equity strategy. “It’s either the boring financial engineering of dividends or share buybacks or it’s a bold move beyond the confines of smartphones, laptops and their associated services and accessories.”
Garnry proposes that Apple (ticker: AAPL) spend just 12 months of its free cash flow to acquire Tesla (TSLA) for $520 a share and get in the driver’s seat of the next frontier of digital innovation. Synergies abound, as the two companies are both heavily vertically integrated, do their own design and engineering, and have upmarket brands. Apple’s financial strength will solve Tesla’s short-term cash-flow issues and allow it to build several new Gigafactories around the world.
Trump tells Powell, “You’re fired.”
The Federal Reserve closes out this year with a fourth quarter-point interest rate hike in December, sending U.S. equities tumbling to start 2019. John Hardy, head of FX strategy at Saxo Bank, predicts an unhappy President Donald Trump facing off against a determined Fed chief Jerome Powell set on clearing bad debts and avoiding an asset bubble caused by premature monetary policy easing.
Once the yield curve inverts, Trump replaces Powell with dovish Minnesota Fed President Neel Kashkari, who floods the U.S. with liquidity to pay for continued government deficits and “beautiful” new infrastructure projects. The result wouldn’t be pretty: “Inflation reaches 6%, is reported at 3%, and the Fed policy is stuck at 1%,” according to Hardy. “That’s deleveraging you can believe in via financial repression to the great detriment of savers.”
The European Union announces a debt jubilee.
According to Christopher Dembik, Saxo’s head of macro analysis, Italy will be unable to meet its debt-refinancing obligations in 2019 as the European Central Bank increases interest rates and a populist revolt presents domestic challenges. European banks suffer, and the EU enters a recession as contagion spreads to France.
With Germany in better shape but intent on preventing the collapse of the euro zone, debt forgiveness is the only remaining option. Dembik predicts a debt jubilee for all debt levels over 50% and a new rule allowing the first 3% of gross domestic product in deficits to be shared among euro-zone countries in 2020.
Corporate credit crunch pushes Netflix into GE’s vortex.
The overextended U.S. corporate bond market implodes in 2019, set off by a General Electric (GE) default, predicts Garnry. GE is forced to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection and sell off assets. “The event sends shockwaves through global credit markets as investors realise that the Federal Reserve’s rate hikes have accidentally tightened financial conditions too much,” wrote Garnry. “Credit spreads over the Treasury curve widen rapidly, painfully lifting funding costs for US companies.”
The corporate bond market is gutted, as investors flee from U.S. high-yield bond exchange-traded funds. Even highflying Netflix (NFLX) isn’t spared, and the streaming giant’s leverage begins to bite. With double the funding costs, Netflix is forced to cut back on new content just as Walt Disney (DIS) enters the market with its own direct-to-consumer streaming service. The result: One of 2018’s best-performing stocks tanks.
Other wild 2019 predictions from the Saxo Team include a devastating solar surge that causes $2 trillion in damage worldwide, a recession in Germany, and the Australian government nationalizing the country’s four biggest banks.
